title: Preparing for amrit
hookLine: many prepare by keeping kesh and the Nitnem for a time
tomorrow: Jasleen's big Sunday. what happens behind that closed door?

cards: Two pieces of advice land on the same night, and they don't match. Simran's dad, Harjit, at the kitchen counter, peeling an orange: don't wait to be perfect, beta. Take it, and amrit gives you the strength to keep it.
Then a text from Jasleen's mom: Jasleen kept the full morning routine for months before she signed up, and that's what made it real. Both of them took amrit. Both love Simran.
And they'd tell her opposite things.

teach.h: PREPARE FIRST: DON'T PROMISE THE UNTRIED.
teach.b: Both views live in Sikh families, so let each make its best case. The first: prepare first. Keep kesh, keep the Nitnem, try the daily life for a time before the ceremony.

Its best case: a vow is a promise to the Guru, and you shouldn't promise what you've never tried. Preparing means the ceremony seals a life that's already begun, and the vow is less likely to crack in week two.

teach.h: TAKE IT AND GROW: HELP FOR THE UNFINISHED.
teach.b: The second: take it and grow. Its best case: amrit isn't a prize for the finished; it's help for the unfinished.
Waiting to feel ready can turn into waiting forever, and the strength people describe comes with the step, not before it. The Granth doesn't set a timetable.

teach.h: ANG 305: RISE EARLY, REMEMBER THE NAME.
teach.b: But Guru Ram Das, on ang 305, describes the day of one who calls himself a Sikh of the Guru: in paraphrase, he rises early, bathes, and remembers the Name, and keeps it close all day.

teach.h: ONE WEEK OF NITNEM, TO SEE.
teach.b: Both sides read that hymn as the goal. They differ only on whether you start living it before the door or after it.
And both would sign the carry: prepare gently. Not a test to cram for. Not a race against Jasleen.
Simran picks one small thing: a week of the full morning Nitnem, just to see what it's like.

how: Some Sikhs keep kesh and the daily banis for a time before taking amrit; others take amrit and grow into the discipline. Families and gurdwaras give different advice.

o: fasting for several days before the ceremony
studying for a written exam on Sikh history
easing into the Sikh daily life before the step

games.q: two ways to prepare — tap the pairs.
p: don't promise what you've never tried
amrit is help for the unfinished
rise early and remember the Name
one week of the morning Nitnem

s: the code sets a fixed preparation period before amrit
no timetable is set; families differ on how long to prepare.
ang 305 describes a Sikh of the Guru rising early to remember the Name
Guru Ram Das: rise early, bathe, remember the Name, keep it close all day.
preparing first means you don't trust the Guru
its best case is the opposite: a vow to the Guru shouldn't be a promise you've never tried.

games.q: your friend says nobody should take amrit until they've kept the whole routine for months. what's the best case for the other side?
o: amrit is help for the unfinished; waiting to feel ready can become waiting forever.
the routine doesn't really matter, so the ceremony is just a tradition.
the code forbids preparing, so practicing first breaks the rules.
games.why: that's the take-it-and-grow view at its strongest. both sides read ang 305's daily rhythm as the goal; they differ on timing.

practice: Choose one practice you'd like to keep for a week, any practice at all. Name the wish in a few words, then the one thing most likely to stop you, then your plan for when it does: if that happens, I'll do this.
Hold the plan in mind for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Preparing for amrit. Trying the daily life before the step, or taking the step and growing into it; either way, gently.

carryVoice: Your line: prepare gently. A week to see what it's like, not a cram session. That's today.

sources.ref: Ang 305 (Gauri ki Var, Guru Ram Das: gur satgur ka jo sikh akhaae su bhalke uth har naam dhiaavai), paraphrased
